cards.front: Recall a key point about Production Processes
cards.back: Job production: one-off, unique products made to customer specification (e.g. custom wedding cake). High quality, high price, but slow and labour-intensive.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Production Processes
cards.back: Batch production: groups of identical products made together (e.g. bakery making 50 loaves). Allows some variety but requires cleaning/resetting between batches.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Production Processes
cards.back: Flow (mass) production: continuous, standardised production on an assembly line (e.g. car manufacturing). High volume, low unit cost, but high set-up costs and inflexible.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Production Processes
cards.back: Productivity measures output per unit of input: labour productivity = output / number of workers. Higher productivity means lower unit costs and greater competitiveness.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Production Processes
cards.back: Lean production aims to minimise waste while maintaining quality: just-in-time (JIT) inventory, kaizen (continuous improvement), and cutting out non-value-added activities.

cards.front: What should you know about business exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating production methods, use the VCAF framework: Volume (how many?), Customisation (how unique?), Automation (how much tech?), Finance (what can the business afford?). The best method depends on market demand and business resources.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Flow production always produces the best-quality products. Correct: Flow production produces consistent products, not necessarily the best quality. Job production typically achieves higher quality because skilled workers focus on each individual item. cards.front: Understanding Production Processes in Business Context
cards.back: Production Processes is a key topic in GCSE Business Studies that affects how businesses operate in the UK economy. Understanding this concept requires knowledge of both theoretical principles and real-world application. The AQA specification requires you to explain, analyse and evaluate business concepts using appropriate terminology, and apply them to real business scenarios using UK examples.

cards.front: Applying Production Processes to UK Business Examples
cards.back: For production processes, applying theory to practice means using real UK business examples to illustrate your understanding. Small businesses face different challenges from large corporations when dealing with production processes. Consider how factors like business size, ownership structure, industry sector and market position affect the impact of production processes on a business.

cards.front: Exam Technique for Production Processes Questions
cards.back: GCSE Business exam questions about production processes range from 1-mark definition questions to 12-mark evaluation questions. For definition questions (1-2 marks), give a precise business definition. For explanation questions (3-4 marks), define and explain with a brief example.
